header.title: Pressure & Partial Pressure
header.subtitle: Understanding how pressure changes with depth and affects the gases you breathe

reading.title: Reading a Dive Profile
reading.text: A dive profile is a graphical representation of your dive, showing depth over time. Understanding the basic terminology helps you communicate with other divers and interpret dive computer data effectively.

descent.label: Descent
descent.text: The phase from leaving the surface until reaching your planned depth. Recommended rate: ≤18-20 m/min.

bottomTime.label: Bottom Time
bottomTime.text: Total time from beginning of descent to start of final ascent. Includes descent phase.

maxDepth.label: Maximum Depth
maxDepth.text: The deepest point reached during the dive. Determines ambient pressure and gas absorption rate.

ascent.label: Ascent
ascent.text: Return to surface. Rate should not exceed 9-10 m/min to prevent bubble formation.

tdt.label: Total Dive Time (TDT)
tdt.text: Complete duration from leaving surface to returning. Includes descent, bottom time, and full ascent.

decoStop.label: Deco Stop
decoStop.text: Mandatory pause at specific depth during ascent to allow safe elimination of inert gases.

safetyStop.label: Safety Stop
safetyStop.text: Voluntary 3-minute pause at 3-5m during ascent to allow excess nitrogen to off-gas safely.

surfaceInterval.label: Surface Interval (SI)
surfaceInterval.text: Time spent at surface between dives to off-gas nitrogen. Longer SI = more nitrogen eliminated.

whatCreates.title: What Creates Pressure Underwater?
whatCreates.intro: The total pressure a diver experiences underwater comes from two sources:
whatCreates.atmospheric: Atmospheric pressure — The weight of the air column above you. At sea level, this is approximately 1 bar (1 atm = 1.01325 bar).
whatCreates.hydrostatic: Hydrostatic pressure — The weight of the water column above you. In seawater, this adds approximately 1 bar per 10 meters of depth.
whatCreates.summary: Therefore, at 10m depth you experience 2 bar total pressure (1 atm + 1 bar water), at 20m it's 3 bar, at 30m it's 4 bar, and so on.

whyDepth.title: Why Depth Matters for Gas Supply
whyDepth.text1: According to Boyle-Mariotte's Law, as pressure increases, the volume of gas decreases proportionally. Underwater, this means you breathe compressed air from your tank. At 10m depth (2 bar), each breath draws twice the amount of gas molecules compared to the surface.
whyDepth.text2: This is why deeper dives consume your gas supply faster—you're breathing the same volume of air, but it contains more gas molecules due to compression.

sac.title: Surface Air Consumption (SAC)
sac.text1: SAC rate (also called RMV - Respiratory Minute Volume) is how much gas you breathe per minute at the surface. For planning purposes, we use a typical value of 20 L/min for relaxed diving, though actual consumption varies based on exertion, stress, and individual factors.
sac.text2: At depth, your actual consumption is: SAC × Ambient Pressure

sacCalc.intro: Knowing your personal SAC rate helps you plan dives more accurately. You can calculate it from real dive data using your pressure drop, cylinder size, dive time, and average depth.
sacCalc.deltaP: Pressure drop (start - end pressure in bar)
sacCalc.examplePressure: Start pressure: 200 bar, End pressure: 80 bar → ΔP = 120 bar
sacCalc.exampleResult: This diver has a SAC rate of 12.8 L/min — quite efficient! Typical recreational divers range from 12-25 L/min depending on fitness, experience, and conditions.
sacCalc.tip1: Use a dive computer that logs average depth, or calculate it from your profile
sacCalc.tip2: Measure over several dives to get a reliable average
sacCalc.tip3: Note that SAC increases with exertion, cold, or stress
sacCalc.tip4: For planning, use a conservative (higher) SAC estimate

whatsInAir.title: What's in the Air You Breathe?
whatsInAir.intro: The air we breathe is a mixture of gases. Understanding this composition is fundamental to diving because each gas behaves differently under pressure. The main components are:
whatsInAir.nitrogen: Nitrogen (N₂) — 78% — inert gas, does not participate in metabolism
whatsInAir.oxygen: Oxygen (O₂) — 21% — essential for life, but toxic at high partial pressures
whatsInAir.other: Other gases — 1% — primarily Argon, CO₂, and trace gases

mixtures.title: Breathing Gas Mixtures
mixtures.intro: Divers use different gas mixtures to manipulate the partial pressures of specific gases at depth. By changing the fraction of each gas in a mix, divers can stay within safe limits for oxygen toxicity and nitrogen narcosis:
mixtures.nitrox: Nitrox (EAN) — Increases the oxygen fraction to lower the partial pressure of nitrogen (ppN2), which reduces nitrogen loading in the tissues.
mixtures.trimix: Trimix — Adds helium to the mix, allowing divers to lower the partial pressures of both oxygen and nitrogen to safe levels for deep diving.

foundation.title: The Foundation of Dive Gas Physics
foundation.text: Dalton's Law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each component gas. The partial pressure of a gas is the pressure it would exert if it occupied the same volume alone.

animation.caption: Each gas (blue, red) exerts its own pressure independently — the total pressure is the sum of all partial pressures.

formula.fx: fraction of gas x in the mixture (decimal, e.g., 0.21 for 21%)
formula.note: Note: This is the operational formula used for MOD and gas limits throughout this section.

operational.intro: There are two common contexts for partial pressure calculations:
operational.opDesc: Used for Maximum Operating Depth (MOD) and oxygen toxicity limits. No water vapour subtraction.
operational.physDesc: When calculating alveolar gas pressures for tissue loading models, we subtract water vapour pressure because the lungs humidify inspired air:
operational.physNote: This ~6% reduction appears in the Bühlmann equations for tissue saturation calculations. We will need this in further sections and stating it here for completeness.

oxygenLimits.title: Oxygen Limits (ppO₂)
oxygenLimits.intro: Oxygen becomes toxic at elevated partial pressures. The body responds differently to various ppO₂ levels:
oxygenLimits.hypoxiaNotes: Loss of consciousness, death. Minimum for survival.
oxygenLimits.safeNotes: Recommended working limit for recreational diving.
oxygenLimits.cautionNotes: Acceptable for decompression stops only. Limited exposure time.
oxygenLimits.dangerNotes: High risk of CNS oxygen toxicity (seizures).

mod.title: Maximum Operating Depth (MOD)
mod.intro: The MOD is the deepest you can safely dive with a specific gas mix without exceeding the ppO₂ limit. It's calculated from the oxygen fraction and desired maximum ppO₂.
mod.exerciseNote: 💡 Notice: higher O₂ fraction → shallower MOD. More oxygen means you hit the toxicity limit sooner.

nitrogenLimits.title: Nitrogen Limits (ppN₂) — Narcosis
nitrogenLimits.intro: Nitrogen becomes narcotic at elevated partial pressures, causing impaired judgment, euphoria, and slowed reactions—similar to alcohol intoxication.
nitrogenLimits.martiniIntro: A popular rule of thumb: every 10 meters of depth on air is roughly equivalent to drinking one martini on an empty stomach. At 30m, you might feel like you've had 3 martinis!
nitrogenLimits.martiniNote: Note: Individual susceptibility varies greatly. Some divers feel effects earlier, others later. Cold, stress, and fatigue increase narcosis.
nitrogenLimits.severe: Severe narcosis. Maximum limit for recreational diving.
nitrogenLimits.exercisesTitle: Exercises: Max depth for narcosis limit
nitrogenLimits.strictNote: ← stricter limit used by some training agencies
nitrogenLimits.exercisesHint: Same formula as MOD, but for nitrogen: Max depth = ((ppN₂<sub>max</sub> / fN₂) − 1) × 10
nitrogenLimits.exerciseNote: 💡 Nitrox pushes the narcosis limit deeper, but the oxygen MOD kicks in first — you always need to respect both limits. The actual limiting factor for EAN mixes is usually oxygen, not narcosis.

cnsOtu.title: CNS & OTU Tracking
cnsOtu.disclaimer: ⚠️ This is advanced content. For recreational diving, simply staying below 1.4 bar ppO₂ is sufficient. CNS/OTU tracking is primarily used in technical diving with extended oxygen exposures.
cnsOtu.cnsDesc: The CNS clock tracks your exposure as a percentage of the maximum allowable time at each ppO₂ level. At 100%, you've reached the recommended limit.

cnsOtu.otuLimits: Daily limits: 300 OTU (single dive), 850 OTU (total daily)

symptoms.warning: ⚠️ If you experience any of these symptoms, immediately signal your buddy and begin ascending. Underwater convulsions are often fatal.
